title: Can a robot nail wall sheathing to code tolerance, and what decides it?
lede: research programme on robotic sheathing of a wood-frame wall; milestone 1: APA's 1/8 in gap shrinks the joint-nail window to ±3.14 mm and sheets must hang plumb to about 0.03°; milestone 2: a bowed stud moves under the straight sheet edge, so at published stud warp a robot reading each stud once gets 55% clean sheets, three reads 80% and perfect sensing 87%, while a 3x or doubled 2x at the joints (as the shear-wall standard allows) gives 100% with three reads; milestone 4: tacking the sheet and aiming from its measured edge lets a robot hang it to 0.54° and 10 mm (1σ) on doubled joints, 18 times coarser than the 0.03° single-2x joints need, where re-hanging tops out at 87% clean
summary: A research programme (proposal and log on the project page) asking whether a stock humanoid, a mobile manipulator with a lift or a purpose-built gantry can hang a 4x8 sheet of wall sheathing and land all 62 nails where the panel maker and the code want them, which error source decides it, and what a clean sheet costs; it gathers track 20's 26 buildbot-* projects into one question aimed at Automation in Construction. Milestone 1 adds what earlier projects left out: panels are hung with a 1/8 in gap (APA's recommendation) centred on the joint stud, sheets are hung slightly off and out of plumb, and their width differs from the 48 in stud module. With the gap, the 34 joint nails' window shrinks from ±3.93 to ±3.14 mm, and the single stud reading needed for 95% clean sheets (0.9 mm tool scatter) falls from 0.90 to 0.41 mm; at buildbot-studfind's 0.89 mm only 75% of sheets come out clean, 56% if the robot does not plan for the gap. With a 0.5 mm stud reading, a robot aiming at the design window has no tolerance for sheet pose at all; aiming from the measured sheet edge (to 0.5 mm) allows 0.44 mm of translation and 0.031° of rotation (1σ), and halves the weight of the stud error. Along a 40 ft wall, sheets butted with a 1/8 in gauge drift 3.2 mm a sheet: no third sheet is clean with full panels, and panels trimmed 1/16 in keep a joint window for four sheets; setting each sheet from its own studs keeps every sheet at 98% clean. Milestone 2 lets the studs bow and twist as real lumber does. A Stud-grade 8 ft 2x4 may bow 3/4 in and twist 3/8 in, and published kiln-dried studs average 0.11–0.21 in of bow and 0.08–0.16 in of twist. Bow moves the 1.5 in nailing face under a sheet edge that stays straight, so a single-2x joint closes for any bow over 0.53 in, whatever the robot knows. At the lower published warp, one read per stud gives 55% clean sheets, three reads and a fitted curve 80%, perfect stud and edge sensing 87%; reaching 95% would mean rejecting about two thirds of studs for bow. Framing the joints with a 3x or two fastened 2x (named for adjoining panel edges in the shear-wall standard, SDPWS 4.3.7.1) widens the window by 1/2 in a side, and three reads then give 100% clean sheets at both warp levels; twist costs 1–2 points. Milestone 4 asks how coarsely a robot may hang the sheet if it tacks it with two field nails, measures where the edge landed and aims the joint nails from that, or re-hangs it when the window looks too tight. On single-2x joints the sheet must still hang to about 0.03° and 0.4 mm (1σ) for 95% clean sheets; re-hanging a 1 mm / 0.1° hang peaks at 87% (2.1 hangs a sheet), and a held sheet may sway only 0.19 mm under the nail. On two 2x fastened at the joint, tack-then-measure allows 0.54° and 10 mm at the lower published warp, and a held sheet may sway 4.1 mm: the placement target for the humanoid and lift experiments. Hang and sway errors are swept, not measured on a robot. Monte Carlo checked against buildbot-studfind and closed forms. Stud, edge, gauge and width errors are swept, not measured; the gap, edge distance and trim come from APA pages seen in search results; stud warp means and limits come from search snippets of USDA and Wood and Fiber reports, the warp distribution shape is assumed (two are shown), and nothing is tested on hardware.
